rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the six-peak elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

The maximum CRF is already achieved, so test a shorter gradient while keeping composition endpoints and temperature fixed. The current minimum resolution of 3.99 provides substantial margin for shortening the separation without losing full resolution.

Test the minimum gradient duration to establish the speed–resolution boundary. The earliest pair may fall below 1.5; if so, the 4-minute gradient remains a fully resolved method with maximum CRF.

Return to the shortest fully resolved gradient and raise temperature to test whether elution can be accelerated while retaining maximum CRF. This also probes temperature-dependent selectivity of the critical early pair.

Higher temperature reduced early-pair selectivity, so test the lowest temperature with the fastest gradient to seek improved resolution. This may recover full resolution at a shorter separation time than the established 4-minute method.

Reduce the gradient slope at the temperature that improved early-pair selectivity, aiming to lift its resolution from 1.31 to at least 1.5. The strong final solvent should still elute all six compounds rapidly, potentially preserving maximum CRF with a faster separation than injection 3.
